verdicts.rationale: The standard's four purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information and ideas) form an OR list; any one student-performed purpose suffices. Students make use of texts — the Patterns of the Stars anchor chart, the book Does the Sun Sleep?, and the Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall — to build knowledge about why stars are not visible during the day. They then share that information and ideas during a Science Talk protocol: "Tell students they will now use their notes to participate in a Science Talk in small groups to answer the question: 'Why can't we see stars during the day?'" Students independently write notes from the texts and use those notes as evidence in group discussion, satisfying both the "build knowledge" and "share information and ideas" purposes. The student is the actor throughout — writing notes, turning and talking, and participating in the Science Talk. [REJECTED: evidence missing or not found in lesson raw text]

clauses.clause: Link ideas and information to an organizational plan. (C)
clauses.note: Students are directed to record notes that link to the organizational plan of answering the guiding question and preparing for the Science Talk, but the 'linking to an organization plan' is loosely scaffolded — students select information from the anchor chart and write notes, but there is no explicit organizational plan (e.g., outline, graphic organizer with sections) to which students deliberately link their ideas.

clauses.clause: Highlight ideas and information that are most relevant, useful, and impactful. (C)
clauses.note: Students are directed to evaluate and select the most important information to include in their notes, performing the highlighting/prioritizing act themselves during turn-and-talk and independent writing.

verdicts.evidence: Remind students that they need to record their notes in a way that is useful to them so that they can read from their notes and use them as evidence in the Science Talk. They should record only the information that they think is most important.
verdicts.rationale: The "highlight ideas and information that are most relevant, useful, and impactful" clause is met: students are asked "What information do you think is most important to know when answering the question 'Why can't we see stars during the day?'" and then independently select and record only the most important information on their notes sheets. The "link ideas and information to an organizational plan" clause is only partially met: students do connect their notes to the purpose of answering the guiding question for the Science Talk, but there is no explicit organizational plan (such as an outline, structured graphic organizer, or sequenced framework) to which students deliberately link and arrange their ideas — the note-taking is loosely guided rather than plan-linked. The gap is the absence of a formal organization plan that students use to structure their writing.

clauses.clause: Offer feedback on peers' writing
Respond to feedback received on own writing

verdicts.evidence: Guide students through the protocol. Circulate and use the Speaking and Listening Checklist to track student progress. Prompt students with questions to help them expand on their ideas.
verdicts.rationale: The lesson partially meets 1.P.EICC.1.e. Students discuss content with others in small-group Science Talks ("Guide students through the protocol… Prompt students with questions to help them expand on their ideas"), share their individual writing by bringing their Patterns of the Stars notes sheets into groups (the teacher notes "Aisha, I saw you show a diagram that you had drawn to your group members"), and listen as others share, evidenced by the sentence frames requiring active listening ("I think he/she means ___," "I'd like to add ___"). However, three clauses are unmet: students do not develop group norms (norms are pre-established and merely reviewed via the anchor chart), students do not offer feedback on peers' writing (the teacher provides feedback, but no student-to-student writing feedback is directed), and students do not respond to feedback on their own writing.

clauses.clause: Determine which text design is most accessible for the intended audience
Decide which word choices and language structures are most effective for the audience and purpose
Identify which craft techniques are most impactful in the text

verdicts.evidence: 'What information do you think is most important to know when answering the question 'Why can't we see stars during the day?'' (Responses will vary, but may include: Stars are very far away, so their light is dim; the sun's light is so bright that it outshines the starlight, etc.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard asks students to draw on authorial knowledge of context and audience across four dimensions: information/ideas to highlight, text design accessibility, word choice/language effectiveness, and craft technique impact. Students do select which information is most important to record for their Science Talk audience ("What information do you think is most important to know when answering the question 'Why can't we see stars during the day?'"), and they are reminded to "record only the information that they think is most important" and to "draw quick sketches that will help them explain," which partially addresses the information-to-highlight clause in a nascent, audience-aware way. However, the lesson never asks students to consider text design accessibility, to evaluate word choices or language structures for effectiveness, or to identify impactful craft techniques. Three of four clauses are unmet, and the one partially met clause lacks explicit framing around authorial audience reasoning.
verdicts.grounding_note: evidence quote found in lesson raw text

clauses.clause: Work with others to solve problems
Work with others to explore and create texts
clauses.note: Students explore texts collaboratively (e.g., reviewing anchor charts, using notes in group discussion), but there is no moment where students collaboratively create a text together; individual note-writing is independent, not collaborative creation.

verdicts.evidence: Guide students through the protocol. Circulate and use the Speaking and Listening Checklist to track student progress. Prompt students with questions to help them expand on their ideas.
verdicts.rationale: The standard decomposes into four clauses joined by commas (an OR-like list of collaborative purposes): discuss topics, investigate questions, solve problems, and explore and create texts. However, re-examining the standard text — "Work with others to discuss topics, investigate questions, solve problems, and explore and create texts" — these are joined by "and," making them separable collaborative acts. Students clearly discuss topics and investigate questions collaboratively during the Science Talk protocol, where they move into small groups and use sentence frames such as "I'd like to add ________" and "This makes me think __________" to build on each other's ideas about why stars can't be seen during the day. No collaborative problem-solving activity is present. Students write notes independently rather than collaboratively creating texts, though they explore shared anchor charts and use notes in group discussion. With two clauses fully met, one partially met, and one not met, the alignment is partial.
